section_path: Article
text: CD47 peptide-cloaked lipid nanoparticles promote cell-specific mRNA delivery

section_path: Abstract
text: mRNA-based therapeutics delivered via lipid nanoparticles (LNP-mRNA) hold great promise for treating diverse diseases. However, further improvements are needed to refine outcomes in non-vaccine, extrahepatic applications, such as minimizing the rapid clearance and off-target uptake in undesired tissues of the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS). We propose modifying LNP surfaces with the phagocytic cell “don’t eat me” signal, CD47, in combination with our previously established antibody-based targeted LNP (tLNP) to create a CD47/tLNP platform with reduced phagocytic clearance and off-target effects and improved efficiency for cell-specific delivery. We showed that CD47 modification decreased macrophage and hepatic uptake both in vitro and in vivo. Combining CD47 modification with antibodies targeting endothelial cells, T cells, or hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) increased targeting efficiency up to 3-fold compared to tLNP alone. Enhanced targeting of CD47/tLNP to HSCs with reduced off-targeting enabled the delivery of pro-apoptotic mRNA for HSC depletion as a preconditioning strategy prior to bone marrow transplant. Additionally, CD47-modified LNPs showed diminished inflammatory effects on hepatic tissue and an altered protein corona. Our CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform, with its reduced phagocytic clearance, mitigated inflammatory effects, and enhanced targeted delivery, should further facilitate the development of in vivo mRNA therapeutics.

section_path: Introduction
text: Lipid nanoparticle encapsulating messenger RNA (LNP-mRNA) has emerged as a promising tool for therapeutic gene delivery in applications such as in vivo chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell production and in vivo hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) gene editing.1,2,3 However, despite the tremendous success of LNP-mRNA technology for vaccine applications, this system still faces challenges in achieving sufficient dosages for extrahepatic applications in vivo, largely due to the innate immune response and phagocytic uptake of LNP-mRNA by cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (MPS).4 Furthermore, while LNP-mRNA are still in the bloodstream, they naturally bind to serum proteins such as apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to form a protein corona, which promotes their uptake by the liver hepatocytes through the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) classical pathway.5,6 Although beneficial for hepatic delivery of therapeutics,7,8 this liver tropism poses a challenge for efficient delivery of LNP-mRNA therapies to non-liver cells in vivo.

section_path: Introduction
text: Following delivery into the bloodstream, the protein corona forms around the LNPs, allowing for increased uptake by the MPS and subsequent processing in the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.9 The MPS consists of immune surveillance cells such as monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, which engulf bacteria, dead tissue cells, and exogenous material. MPS cells widely express the phagocytosis regulatory marker, signal regulatory protein-α (SIRP-α) on their surface.10 The anti-phagocytic counterpart of SIRP-α is transmembrane protein CD47, which is a recognition molecule acting as a ubiquitous “don’t eat me” signal found on cell surfaces.10

section_path: Introduction
text: A beneficial aspect of the LNP-mRNA platform is the modular nature of LNP composition and surface modification. For example, we have shown in previous work that LNP-mRNA can be conjugated with targeting antibodies to enable delivery to specific cell types in vivo following intravenous (i.v.) administration, such as HSCs,3 T cells,2 lung endothelium,11 and inflamed brain vasculature.12 We hypothesize that incorporating the CD47 peptide onto the surface of targeted LNP (tLNP)-mRNA will reduce their uptake and clearance by the MPS, alter the protein corona to minimize unwanted hepatic uptake, and thereby enhance the targeted delivery of mRNA to specific cell types.

section_path: Introduction
text: Here, we report on the development and evaluation of CD47 peptide-cloaked LNP-mRNA (CD47/LNP-mRNA), which resulted in a substantial decrease in uptake of LNP-mRNA by the phagocytic system and a reduction in biodistribution in the liver. We then examined the impact of CD47 modification of LNP on in vivo cell targeting by co-conjugating CD47/LNP-mRNA with antibodies targeting endothelial cells (CD47+aCD31/tLNP-mRNA), T cells (CD47+aCD4/tLNP-mRNA), and HSCs (CD47+aCD117/tLNP-mRNA).2,3,11 Through biodistribution experiments, we found a prominent expression boost in targeted tissues and a reduction in off-target effects in the liver. We also demonstrated that CD47/LNP-mRNA evades pro-inflammatory pathways, as evidenced by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) assays. The presented immune-evasive CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform offers a promising tool for enhanced efficacy of targeted mRNA therapeutics.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification of LNP-mRNA promotes macrophage evasion in vitro and reduces liver uptake in vivo
text: We first modified the surface of LNP-mRNA with CD47 peptide to generate CD47/LNP-mRNA (Figure 1A). To assess CD47 peptide grafting density on LNPs, we first determined the total particle count in 1 μg (by mRNA) of CD47/LNP-mRNA as 7.5E+11 using the ZetaView TWIN instrument. We then measured the average CD47 peptide content via the ultra-sensitive CBQCA protein quantification assay. The number of CD47 peptides per LNP was calculated as 8.9 (±0.5), and the grafting efficiency was calculated as 89.4% (Figure S1). To assess whether CD47 peptide incorporation would alter the physical properties of LNPs, we compared the particle size, polydispersity index, and zeta potential of LNP encapsulating green fluorescent protein (GFP) mRNA (LNP-GFP) with vs. without CD47 peptide modification, using a Malvern Zetasizer. We found that incorporation of the CD47 peptide did not significantly increase the size of the LNP (Figure 1B, 76.8 ± 0.4 vs. 75.7 ± 0.3 nm). Similarly, the polydispersity index showed no substantial change. Interestingly, the zeta potential of CD47-modified LNPs is slightly closer to neutral (2.72 ± 1.82 vs. −6.88 ± 0.52), which may be a benefit to less non-specific interactions with blood components.13,14,15,16 To examine the potential of CD47/LNP-mRNA to evade phagocytic uptake in vitro, we delivered unmodified LNP-mRNA, CD47/LNP-mRNA, or SIRP-α blockade + CD47/LNP-mRNA, where the mRNA encoded GFP (LNP-GFP), to the SIRP-α expressing mouse macrophage cell line RAW 264.7.17 The SIRP-α blockade was performed by incubating the cells with 20 μg/mL SIRP-α blockade antibody in full medium for 2 h at 37°C before the LNP treatment. At 24 h after treatment, we imaged the cells and found that cells transfected with CD47/LNP-GFP showed a substantial decrease in GFP expression, suggesting that CD47 modification reduced macrophage uptake of LNP-mRNA (Figure 1C, two center panels). The reduction of GFP expression was partially reversed by SIRP-α blockade (Figure 1C, right panel). Further quantitative analysis with flow cytometry showed that while CD47 peptide incorporation significantly reduced GFP mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) by 75% (6,419 vs. 24,841 relative fluorescence units [RFU]), SIRP-α blockade rescued this reduction (13,032 RFU) (Figures 1D and 1E). These data indicate that the impact of CD47 peptide on LNP uptake is largely through the CD47-SIRP-α interaction.Figure 1CD47/LNP-mRNA evades macrophage recognition in vitro and liver uptake in vivo(A) Schematic of decorations of LNP-mRNA with CD47 peptide. (B) Physical properties of LNP with vs. without CD47 peptide incorporation. (C) Wide-field microscopy images of RAW 264.7 cells incubated with LNP-GFP, CD47/LNP-GFP, or SIRP-α blockade+CD47/LNP-GFP. Scale bar, 100 μm. (D) The GFP expression level in each indicated group. (E) The MFI of GFP signal in GFP+ cells in each indicated group (n = 3). Data are represented as mean (SD). Two-sided Student’s t test, ∗∗p < 0.01; ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. (F) Schematic of radiolabeled LNP biodistribution in vivo assay. (G) Biodistribution of radiolabeled unmodified LNP-mRNA and CD47/LNP-mRNA in mice at T = 4 h. Tissue uptake is indicated as mean (SEM) (n = 3). Mann-Whitney U test; ∗∗p < 0.01. (H) Localization ratio as %ID/g in selected organs in mice treated with unmodified LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA normalized to blood levels. Mann-Whitney U test; ∗∗p < 0.01. (I) IVIS bioluminescence imaging of tissues from mice treated with either unmodified LNP-Luc or CD47/LNP-Luc measured at T = 4 h. (J) Total flux (p/s) quantification of respective organs of interest.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification of LNP-mRNA promotes macrophage evasion in vitro and reduces liver uptake in vivo
text: To evaluate how CD47 modification affects the biodistribution of LNP-mRNA in vivo, we radiolabeled unmodified LNP-mRNA and CD47/LNP-mRNA with Na125I for particle biodistribution analysis (Figure 1F). LNP-mRNA were administered i.v. into C57BL/6 mice. Four hours post-administration, tissues were harvested and prepared for radioactivity counting. In per gram of blood, CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice showed a retention rate of ∼20% of the injected dosage (ID/g), compared to only about 4% ID/g in unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice. Additionally, CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice exhibited a ∼6-fold decrease in liver uptake and a ∼3-fold decrease in spleen uptake compared to those treated with unmodified LNP-mRNA (Figure 1G). Next, we assessed the localization ratio (LR) in the liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and heart (Figure 1H). LR measures the organ-to-blood ratio of LNP uptake, allowing for a comparison of biodistribution while accounting for differences in blood clearance.11,12 The LR of unmodified LNP-mRNA compared to CD47/LNP-mRNA was significantly higher in the liver by ∼23-fold and in the spleen by ∼11-fold (Mann-Whitney U test, ∗∗p < 0.01). These in vivo results indicate that CD47 modification reduces hepatic and splenic uptake of LNPs.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification of LNP-mRNA promotes macrophage evasion in vitro and reduces liver uptake in vivo
text: To further assess how CD47 modification affects LNP-mRNA biodistribution and protein expression, we generated CD47-modified LNP-luciferase mRNA (CD47/LNP-Luc) for in vivo imaging system (IVIS) bioluminescence analysis. Mice were i.v. injected with 10 μg unmodified LNP-Luc or CD47/LNP-Luc. Four hours later, the organs were harvested and prepared for imaging (Figure 1I). In the CD47-modified group, the liver showed a ∼3-fold decrease in luciferase activity, and the spleen showed a ∼2-fold decrease, as measured by total flux photons per second (p/s) (Figure 1J). These data suggest that CD47 modification reduces mRNA delivery and expression to the liver and spleen.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification enhances the efficiency of tLNP-mRNA
text: Conjugating cell-targeting antibodies to LNP-mRNA to yield tLNP-mRNA has been demonstrated as an effective approach for tissue- or cell-specific delivery of mRNAs.2,3,11,12,18,19 As CD47 modification reduces liver uptake, we hypothesize that incorporating CD47 modification into tLNPs (CD47/tLNP-mRNA) could augment targeted delivery of mRNA. To evaluate tissue specificity and in vivo targeting efficiency of CD47/tLNP-mRNA, we sought to target lung endothelium using anti-CD31 antibody, as previously reported.11 First, anti-mouse CD31 antibody was conjugated to CD47/LNP-Luc (Figure 2A). Then, we performed IVIS bioluminescence imaging of harvested tissues from mice treated with 10 μg aCD31/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD31/tLNP-Luc. The CD47-modified LNP-Luc group demonstrated a boosted luciferase expression in the lung and a reduced expression in liver and spleen (Figures 2B and 2C). To quantitatively assess the difference of tissue uptake of tLNP with vs. without CD47, we measured the luciferase activity per milligram protein in the desired organs and found lung-specific luciferase expression increased from 1.5E+6 LU/mg protein in the unmodified group to 2E+6 LU/mg protein in the CD47-modified group, demonstrating a ∼33% enhancement; in contrast, liver and spleen uptake was significantly reduced in the CD47-modified group (Figure S2). To assess whether elevated lung uptake reflects an enhanced delivery to the lung CD31+ endothelial cells, we injected 1 μg aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen or CD47+aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen into the mice i.v.; then, we harvested and dissociated lungs 24 h post-treatment to measure ZsGreen expression in CD45−CD31+ endothelial cells. Mice treated with aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen showed an average of 8.3% ZsGreen+ in the CD45−CD31+ population, which significantly increased to 17.0% with the addition of the CD47 peptide (Figures 2D and 2E), indicating that CD47 modification enhances endothelial cell targeting.Figure 2CD47 modification enhances endothelial and T cell-targeting efficiency(A) Schematic of conjugating anti-CD31 or anti-CD4 antibodies to CD47/LNP-mRNA for enhanced targeting to endothelial cells or CD4+ T cells. (B) IVIS bioluminescence imaging of mice treated with either CD47+aCD31/tLNP-Luc or aCD31/tLNP-Luc, measured at T = 4 h. (C) Total flux (p/s) quantification of respective organ ROI. (D) Flow cytometry analysis of ZsGreen expression in CD31+ endothelial cells isolated from the lungs of mice 24 h post-treatment with either 1 μg CD47+aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen or aCD31/tLNP-ZsGreen intravenously (i.v.). (E) Quantification of ZsGreen+ percentage within CD31+ lung endothelial cells (n = 2 for untreated, n = 5 for other groups). (F) IVIS bioluminescence imaging of mice treated with either CD47+aCD4/tLNP-Luc or aCD4/tLNP, measured at T = 4 h. (G) Total flux (p/s) quantification of respective organ ROI. (H) ZsGreen expression in splenic CD4+ T cells (CD3+CD8−) isolated from mice 24 h post-treatment with either 1 μg CD47+aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen or aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen i.v. (I) Quantification of ZsGreen+ percentage within splenic CD4+ T cells (n = 2 for untreated, n = 4 for other groups). Data are represented as mean (SEM). Two-sided Student’s t test; ∗p < 0.05; ∗∗p < 0.01.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification enhances the efficiency of tLNP-mRNA
text: In parallel, to test whether CD47 modification can enhance delivery of aCD4/tLNP that targets CD4+ T cells,2,11,20,21,22 we first injected 10 μg aCD4/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD4/tLNP-Luc into the mice i.v. and then measured luciferase expression in the liver and spleen. We found enhanced mRNA expression in the spleen and reduced mRNA expression in the liver in mice injected with CD47+aCD4/tLNP-Luc (Figures 2F and 2G). To directly evaluate the T cell-targeting efficiency of CD47-modified tLNP, we injected 1 μg CD47+aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen or unmodified aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen into the mice i.v. and harvested the spleen 24 h after the flow cytometry analysis of ZsGreen expression in T cells. Mice treated with aCD4/tLNP-ZsGreen showed an average of 46.6% ZsGreen+ in CD4+ T cells, which increased to 51.1% with the addition of the CD47 peptide (Figures 2H and 2I), indicating that CD47 modification enhances CD4+ T cell targeting. In summary, these data suggest that co-decorating antibody-modified targeted LNP with CD47 peptide have the potential to enhance the efficiency of targeted delivery.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification enables in vivo depletion of HSCs with HSC-targeted LNP encapsulating apoptotic mRNA by reducing off-target effects
text: Depleting existing HSCs is a prerequisite for standard bone marrow transplant (BMT) therapy. In our prior study, we showcased using aCD117/tLNP-Puma mRNA for in vivo HSC depletion,3 which could overcome the adverse side effects associated with conventional approaches (i.e., chemotherapy, radiation). Despite the potent depletion of HSCs with aCD117/tLNP-Puma, this agent also caused toxicity due to off-target uptake by the liver.23 We hypothesize that incorporating CD47 modification on the aCD117/tLNP-Puma would diminish Puma-induced liver toxicity while retaining its HSC depletion function (Figure 3A). To explore this hypothesis, we first asked whether CD47 modification could reduce the liver uptake of aCD117/tLNP-mRNA while preserving its ability to target the BM. We injected 1 μg of aCD117/tLNP-Luc or CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Luc in the mice and then imaged luciferase biodistribution in the liver and whole-femur BM using IVIS. In the absence of HSCs-targeting element aCD117, CD47 modification potently reduced liver expression of luciferase (CD47+immunoglobulin G (IgG)/tLNP vs. IgG/tLNP), but without luciferase expression in the BM. When aCD117 was added to the surface of LNPs, CD47 modification not only reduced luciferase expression in liver but also enhanced expression in the BM (Figure 3B). To further evaluate the delivery efficiency of CD47+aCD117/tLNP to HSCs at the cellular level in vivo, we administered 1 μg CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Cre or aCD117/tLNP-Cre to Ai6 mice, which contain a loxP reporter system to express ZsGreen upon Cre-mediated recombination (Figure 3C). At T = 24 h, animals were euthanized, femurs were removed, and BM was processed to a single cell suspension for flow cytometric analysis. Compared with aCD117/tLNP-Cre, CD47-modified tLNPs yielded significantly higher ZsGreen+ proportion in the Lin−Sca1+CD117+ HSCs, boosting ∼3-fold from 6.9% to 22.2% (Figures 3D and 3E).Figure 3CD47 modification combined with aCD117/tLNP containing Puma mRNA reduces off-target Puma-induced toxicity and enables bone marrow transplantation (BMT)(A) CD47-modified aCD117/tLNP-Puma for in vivo HSC depletion with reduced off-target Puma-induced toxicity. (B) IVIS imaging of liver, spleen, and BM 4 h after treating mice with 1 μg of either control IgG/LNP-Luc, CD47+IgG/LNP-Luc, aCD117/tLNP-Luc, or CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Luc. (C) Ai6 mice bearing a Cre/loxP reporter system that induces ZsGreen expression upon Cre recombination to produce ZsGreen+ HSCs. (D) ZsGreen expression in HSCs from Ai6 mice 24 h post-treatment with 1 μg CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Cre or aCD117/tLNP-Cre. (E) Quantification of ZsGreen+ percentage in HSCs (n = 3). Data are represented as mean (SEM). Two-sided Student’s t test; ∗∗∗p < 0.001. (F) Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of mice treated with 1 μg CD47+aCD117/LNP-Puma (n = 7). Log rank test; ∗∗p < 0.01. (G) Percentage of GFP+ engrafted cells in CD45+, CD19+, CD3+, and Gr1+ populations of the PB after 4 months of BMT. (H) Percentage of GFP+ engrafted cells in granulocytes and RBC populations of the PB 2 weeks after BMT.

section_path: Results > CD47 modification enables in vivo depletion of HSCs with HSC-targeted LNP encapsulating apoptotic mRNA by reducing off-target effects
text: We further asked whether the reduction in liver uptake by CD47 modification is sufficient to mitigate the Puma-induced toxicity of aCD117/tLNP-Puma. Compared to mice treated with unmodified aCD117/tLNP-Puma (1 μg), those treated with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma exhibited a substantially higher survival rate 7 days after treatment (Figure 3F; 100% vs. 35%, ∗∗p < 0.01). We then tested in vivo HSC depletion with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma as pre-conditioning for BMT. The donor HSCs carry a permanent GFP reporter, enabling the evaluation of engraftment level by measuring GFP in blood cells. Four months post-BMT, mice preconditioned with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma resulted in prominently higher GFP expression in the CD45+, CD19+, CD3+, and GR1+ blood-derived monocyte populations, compared to those preconditioned with aCD117/tLNP-Puma (Figure 3G), suggesting a higher HSC depletion efficacy with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma. Nevertheless, the GFP+ cells constitute only a minor fraction (∼0.5%), which could be attributed to the incomplete depletion of the recipient’s HSC and the equal competence (if not higher) of the remaining recipient HSCs and the transferred HSCs. Indeed, when we analyzed the percentage of GFP+ blood cells at a much earlier time point (2 weeks post-BMT) compared to the 4-month time point, we observed a higher percentage of GFP+ granulocytes (∼1.5%) and a comparable percentage of GFP+ red blood cells (RBCs) in mice preconditioned with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma (Figure 3H). In the future, the BMT regimen will be further optimized by increasing CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma dosage for preconditioning and the quantity of transferred HSCs. Nonetheless, we demonstrated that CD47 modification is a promising strategy to reduce the Puma-induced liver toxicity by using aCD117/tLNP-Puma for preconditioning of BMT.

section_path: Results > CD47-modified LNP shows mitigated inflammatory effects and altered protein corona
text: Peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) recruitment is an indicator of inflammatory stimuli.24 To test whether CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory than unmodified LNPs, we compared PBMC counts in mice treated with either unmodified LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA after i.v. injection. We found that the PBMC counts from CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice are comparable to those of untreated mice (∼5E+6 vs. ∼3E+6 PBMC/mL). In contrast, PBMC counts from unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice showed a 10-fold increase (∼3E+7 cells/mL) (Figure 4A) when compared to untreated mice. These data indicate that CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory compared to unmodified LNP-mRNA. Our previous work showed that LNP-mRNA administration exaggerates pre-existing inflammation.16 To further test whether CD47-modified LNP-mRNA are less inflammatory than unmodified LNP-mRNA, we treated mice with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to induce an inflammatory state, followed by the administration of CD47/LNP-mRNA or unmodified LNP-mRNA; then, we assessed the level of pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the serum. ELISA assays showed a significantly lower IL-6 level in the serum of CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated mice compared to those treated with unmodified LNP-mRNA (Figure 4B), further suggesting that CD47-modified LNP-mRNA is less inflammatory.Figure 4Effect of CD47 modification on total liver transcriptome and protein corona composition(A) PBMC count/mL from PB at T = 24 h post-injection of unmodified LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA. (B) LPS was administered i.v. at 2 mg/kg to induce systemic inflammation. At T = 4 h, mice were treated with 0.3 mg/kg unmodified LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA i.v. At T = 8 h, serum was processed, and IL-6 concentration was measured by ELISA analysis. Data are represented as mean (SEM). Two-sided Student’s t test; ∗p < 0.05. (C) RNA-seq analysis of liver tissues from mice treated with unmodified LNP-mRNA (NP0), CD47/LNP-mRNA (NP1), and scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA (NP2), compared with untreated (n = 3). (D) LC-MS-based proteomic heatmap analysis of protein coronas formed with scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA, unmodified LNP-mRNA, or CD47/LNP-mRNA.

section_path: Results > CD47-modified LNP shows mitigated inflammatory effects and altered protein corona
text: Since unmodified LNP-mRNA mainly accumulates in the liver, we explored liver responses to CD47-modified LNP-mRNA by performing RNA-seq on liver samples from C57BL/6 mice 4 h after i.v. administration of 10 μg unmodified LNP-mRNA, CD47/LNP-mRNA, or scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA. The differential gene expression analysis indicates a significant downregulation of 30 genes, ranging from −18.40 to −2.11-fold in CD47/LNP-mRNA-treated and untreated mice compared to unmodified LNP-mRNA-treated mice (Figure 4C). Eight genes belong to the acute phase response (APR) pro-inflammatory protein family, including Saa3,25 Timp1,26 Plscr1,27 Cxcl9,28 Cd14,29 Hamp,30 Hpx,31 and Serpina10.32 Notably, the most differentially expressed gene, Saa3, which is downregulated by a fold change of −18.40 (p = 1E−7) in the CD47-modified group, is a murine APR apolipoprotein gene produced in hepatic or extrahepatic tissues and responds to systemic pro-inflammatory stimulation.33,34 Other genes, including Gbp2,35 Gbp6,36 Bmper,37 and Id1,38 involved in phagocytosis, autophagy, and endocytosis, were also significantly downregulated in the CD47-modified group. Principal-component analysis39 showed that the CD47-modified group clustered close to the untreated mice compared to the unmodified LNP-mRNA group (Figure S3). Together, these RNA-seq data indicate that CD47-modified LNP-mRNA reduces acute inflammatory responses in the liver.

section_path: Results > CD47-modified LNP shows mitigated inflammatory effects and altered protein corona
text: It is known that LNP-mRNA in the bloodstream interacts with serum biomolecules to form a surface protein corona, which critically affects the clearance rate and biodistribution of the LNP-mRNA.14,40,41,42 To assess whether CD47 modification alters the protein corona, we analyzed the composition of the protein corona formed surrounding CD47/LNP-mRNA, control scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA, or unmodified LNP-mRNA. The LNP-mRNA variants were incubated with normal mouse serum at a 1:1 ratio for 1 h at 37°C. Then, protein coronas were isolated through column chromatography, as previously reported,43 followed by LC-MS analysis. We identified a total of 41 proteins that were differentially adsorbed among the LNP-mRNA groups (Figure 4D). In the corona of CD47-modified LNP, apolipoproteins Apoa2 and Apoe were significantly less abundant, with an Apoe Z score of −0.04 in the CD47-modified LNP compared to 1.02 in the unmodified LNP. The Apoe is known to promote hepatic uptake of LNP through binding to LDLRs on liver cells and facilitate clearance of LNP from the bloodstream into the liver. In accordance, Apoc3 and Apoc4, which act as antagonists to Apoe and inhibit liver uptake of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins via LDLRs, were found to be elevated in the protein corona of CD47-modified LNP.44,45,46,47,48,49 Notably, CD47/LNP-mRNA also shows an increased affinity for serum albumin (Albu), the most abundant plasma protein that has been shown to increase the retention of LNPs in the bloodstream, with a Z score of 1.11 compared to −0.28 in unmodified LNP. The decreased interaction with Apoe and increased binding to Albu may underlie the reduced liver uptake of CD47-modified LNP-mRNA, as shown in Figures 1F–1J.

section_path: Discussion
text: LNP-mRNA platform technology may still face clinical barriers when it comes to systemic delivery of mRNA therapeutics. This includes, but is not limited to, the high cellular uptake by the MPS and inherent preferential hepatic tropism. Another barrier is the subsequent activation of the innate immune response that hinders the bioavailability of therapeutic mRNA cargo to the target cells.50,51 Therefore, improving LNP delivery to extrahepatic tissues is critical for mRNA therapeutic development. tLNP has emerged as a promising mRNA delivery system for in vivo therapeutics and gene therapy, offering superior tissue and cell specificity.1,2,3,52,53,54 However, this system still suffers from off-target mRNA expression. Here, we demonstrate that the surface decoration of LNP-mRNA with CD47 self-peptide, along with cell-targeting antibodies, substantially boosted mRNA delivery in three target cell types of interest in vivo—T cells, lung endothelial cells, and HSCs.

section_path: Discussion
text: We demonstrated in vivo that CD47/LNP-mRNA decreased hepatic uptake compared to unmodified LNPs. We then tested the tissue-targeting capability of CD47/LNP-mRNA by co-conjugating with anti-CD31, anti-CD4, or anti-CD117 antibodies for systemic delivery. We showed that the resulting CD47/tLNP-mRNAs led to significantly higher levels of mRNA delivery and expression in each target cell. We then evaluated the potential of CD47+aCD117/tLNP-mRNA in HSC targeting and to switch on a Cre/loxP-mediated reporter system. Through RNA-seq and serum pro-inflammatory cytokine analyses, we found that CD47/LNP-mRNA induces a lower pro-inflammatory response in hepatic tissue compared to non-modified LNP-mRNA; particularly the genes within the APR pathway were downregulated. It is worthy of note that the CD47 modification also contributes to a 5-fold increase of LNP-mRNA presence in the bloodstream upon administration. The data from the protein corona composition analysis of a corona surrounding CD47/LNP-mRNA indicate that such an increase may likely be attributed to the composition of its serum protein corona and reduced affinity for Apoe, an important protein for shuttling LNP-mRNA to the liver.55 We observed significantly increased targeting efficiency of CD47/tLNP-mRNA, including a 150% increase in lung targeting efficiency of CD47+aCD31/tLNP-mRNA over aCD31/tLNP-mRNA. We also showed that CD47 modification enables a novel method of HSC depletion via the targeted delivery of cytotoxic Puma mRNA. Current genotoxic conditioning regimen causes substantial pulmonary, liver, and reproductive toxicity.56,57,58 HSC depletion with CD47+aCD117/tLNP-Puma ameliorated the Puma-induced toxicity from non-specific uptake observed by aCD117/tLNP-Puma and empowered successful engraftment and hematopoiesis after BMT.

section_path: Discussion
text: CD47/LNP-mRNA shares many of the same immune-evasive and pharmacokinetic properties as the first CD47-coated polyethylene glycol (PEG) nanobeads developed for in vivo drug delivery by Rodriguez et al. in 2013.59 They showed that CD47-coated PEG nanobeads suppressed clearance by macrophages and prolonged circulation relative to PEG nanobead controls. Similarly, Milani et al. developed a CD47-overexpressing lentiviral vector that inhibited phagocytosis and reduced acute inflammatory responses in non-human primates.60 Additionally, SIRP-α-expressing macrophages, Kupffer cells (KCs), which reside in the liver, account for ∼15% of the total liver cell population.61,62 We, therefore, hypothesize that CD47 modification could suppress the phagocytic uptake of LNP-mRNA by KCs, leading to an overall reduction of mRNA signal in the liver. Furthermore, recent studies have shown that the knockdown of CD47 in cancer cells results in increased phagocytosis by KCs.63

section_path: Discussion
text: Our previous studies have demonstrated a wide spectrum of applications of antibody-targeted LNP-mRNA in gene therapy, such as in vivo CAR-T cell production, in vivo gene editing, and in vivo delivery of functional mRNAs to HSCs.1,3 This study describes a peptide-cloaked LNP-mRNA platform that incorporates a “don’t eat me” CD47 signal into LNP-mRNA. This modification effectively reduces the non-specific uptake of LNP by the mononuclear phagocytic system and mitigates the pro-inflammatory aspects of LNP in vivo. As a result, our platform significantly enhances the bioavailability of mRNA cargoes to the intended targeted cells, thereby improving the efficacy of mRNA delivery and reducing unwanted off-target effects. The CD47/tLNP-mRNA platform presented here could pave the way for precise delivery of LNP-mRNA-based therapeutics across a broad spectrum of diseases.

section_path: Materials and methods > Ethics statement
text: The investigators faithfully adhered to the “Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals” by the Committee on Care of Laboratory Animal Resources Commission on Life Sciences, National Research Council. The animal facilities at the University of Pennsylvania are fully accredited by the American Association for Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care.

section_path: Materials and methods > Ethics statement
text: All studies were conducted under protocols approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Animal treatments were approved by the IACUC at the University of Pennsylvania and the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. Reporting of animal studies has been provided in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines.

section_path: Materials and methods > Mice
text: Equal numbers of male and female C57BL/6J mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory for this study. Ai6 (RCL-ZsGreen) mice on C57BL/6J background were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (stock no. 007906). Ai6 is a Cre reporter allele that has a loxP-flanked STOP cassette preventing transcription of a CAG promoter-driven enhanced GFP (EGFP) variant (ZsGreen1), all inserted into the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus. Upon Cre-mediated recombination, Ai6 mice robustly express ZsGreen1 fluorescence.

section_path: Materials and methods > mRNA production and formulation into LNPs
text: mRNAs were produced as previously described,2,11 using T7 RNA polymerase MegaScript kit (Thermo Fisher) on linearized plasmids encoding firefly luciferase (Luc2), Cre recombinase (Cre), or EGFP. Gene sequences for Luc2, Cre, and EGFP were sourced from SnapGene (www.snapgene.com/resources) plasmids pGL4.10 [luc2], pCMV6-Entry-Cre, and pEGFP, respectively, and then codon optimized. The Puma gene was sourced from NCBI reference sequence NM_133234.3 and then codon optimized.

section_path: Materials and methods > mRNA production and formulation into LNPs
text: To generate modified nucleoside-containing mRNA, m1ψ−5′-triphosphate (TriLink) was incorporated in place of uridine triphosphate nucleosides. mRNAs were transcribed to contain 101-nt-long poly(A) tails. The mRNAs were capped using the m7G capping kit, with 2′-O-methyltransferase ScriptCap (CellScript) to obtain cap1, or capping of the in vitro transcribed mRNAs was performed co-transcriptionally using the trinucleotide cap1 analog CleanCap (TriLink). mRNA was purified by cellulose purification, as described previously.64 All prepared RNAs were analyzed by electrophoresis using denaturing or native agarose gels and stored at −20°C.

section_path: Materials and methods > mRNA production and formulation into LNPs
text: Cellulose-purified m1ψ-containing mRNAs were encapsulated using a self-assembly process described previously.65 Briefly, an ethanolic lipid mixture of ionizable cationic lipid, phosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and PEG-lipid was mixed rapidly with an aqueous solution containing the mRNA at acidic pH. The ionizable lipid is proprietary to Acuitas Therapeutics. The mRNA-loaded LNPs were characterized by dynamic light scattering using a Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments) and a Quant iT Ribogreen assay (Thermo Fisher). The mean hydrodynamic diameter of these LNP-mRNAs was ∼80 nm, with a polydispersity index of 0.02–0.06 and an encapsulation efficiency of ∼95%.

section_path: Materials and methods > Preparation of CD47 and monoclonal antibody-conjugated LNPs
text: Custom CD47 peptide containing the sequence of “GNYTCEVTELSREGKTVIELK” was synthesized by LifeTein. Micelles containing the CD47 peptide were incorporated into LNPs via post-insertion mixing.66 LNPs were decorated with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) specific for mouse CD4, CD31, CD117, IgG isotype control, and/or CD47 peptide for further experiments. To prepare targeted LNPs, purified rat anti-mouse CD4, clone RM4-5 (BioLegend), purified rat anti-mouse CD31, clone MEC13.3 (BioLegend), purified rat anti-mouse CD117, clone 2B8 (BioLegend), or purified rat IgG isotype control (Thermo Fisher) mAbs were coupled to LNP-mRNA via N-succinimidyl S-acetylthioacetate (SATA)-maleimide conjugation chemistry, as described previously.1,3,11 Briefly, LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA was modified with maleimide functioning groups (DSPE-PEG-mal) by a post-insertion technique. The mAb was functionalized with SATA (Thermo Fisher) to introduce sulfhydryl groups, allowing conjugation to maleimide. SATA was deprotected using 0.5 M hydroxylamine, followed by the removal of the unreacted components by Zeba spin desalting columns (ThermoFisher). The reactive sulfhydryl group on the antibody was then conjugated to maleimide moieties using thioether conjugation chemistry. Purification was done using Sepharose CL-4B gel filtration columns (MilliporeSigma). mRNA content was quantified by performing a modified Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA assay (Thermo Fisher). After addition of the targeting ligand, all the targeted and non-targeted LNP preparations were stored at 4°C and were used within 3 days of preparation.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell culture
text: Mouse macrophage RAW 264.7 cells were purchased from American Type Culture Collection and maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (Life Technologies). RAW 264.7 cells were transfected with 10 μg CD47/LNP-GFP or LNP-GFP for 18 h prior to capturing through the wide-field microscopy technique. To block SIRP-α before LNP transfection, RAW264.7 cells were first incubated with 20 μg/mL of SIRP-α blockade antibody (Bio X Cell, catalog no. BE0322) in full medium for 2 h at 37°C. Then, the medium was replaced with fresh medium to remove excess antibody before transfection.

section_path: Materials and methods > Biodistribution studies upon i.v. administration of radiolabeled LNP-mRNA in mice
text: LNP-mRNA was radiolabeled with Na125I using iodination beads (Pierce) as previously described.11 The reaction was performed for 15 min at room temperature. Unreacted radiolabeled materials were subsequently removed via G-25 Sephadex Quick Spin Protein Columns (Roche). Radiolabeled LNP-mRNAs were administered by i.v. retro-orbital injection in C57BL/6 mice under isoflurane anesthesia (all injection treatments were performed i.v. under isoflurane anesthesia). Animals were sacrificed at T = 4 h post-injection, and their blood was collected from the inferior vena cava. Organs (liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and heart) were harvested, rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), blotted dry, and weighed individually. Tissue radioactivity in organs and 100-μL blood samples was measured in a Wallac 1470 gamma counter (Wizard). Radioactivity values and weight of the samples were then used to calculate targeting parameters of the LNPs, including tissue uptake as a percentage of %ID/g tissue and LR as an organ-to-blood ratio. These parameters were employed to examine the pharmacokinetics of biodistribution and effectiveness of antibody-targeted formulation uptake in desired tissue.

section_path: Materials and methods > Collection of PBMCs from mice
text: CD47/LNP-mRNA, unmodified LNP-mRNA, or PBS was administered to the mice i.v. by retro-orbital injection. Animals were sacrificed at T = 4 h post-injection; blood was collected from the vena cava through cardiac puncture, and PBMCs were isolated. PBMCs were then processed and counted using hemocytometer through bright-field microscopy.

section_path: Materials and methods > Biodistribution of radiolabeled CD47/LNP-mRNA in C57BL/6J mice and luciferase mRNA translation activity in mouse tissues
text: C57BL/6J mice were administered radiolabeled Na125I LNP-Luc.2,11,12 At T = 4 h post-injection, animals were euthanized, and selected organs (liver, spleen, lung, kidneys, and heart) were harvested, rinsed with PBS, or stored at −80°C until analysis. For radiolabeled biodistribution, organs were blotted dry and weighed individually. Tissue radioactivity in organs and 100-μL blood samples was measured in a Wallac 1470 gamma counter (Wizard). For luciferase activity, tissues were frozen at −80°C. When thawed, tissue samples were homogenized in appropriate volumes of cell lysis buffer (1×) (Promega) containing protease inhibitor cocktail (1×) and mixed gently at 4°C for 1 h. The homogenates were then subjected to cycles of freeze/thaw in dry ice/37°C and centrifuged for 10 min at 16,000 × g at 4°C. Luciferase activity was then measured in the supernatant using a Victor 3 1420 Multilabel Plate Counter (PerkinElmer).

section_path: Materials and methods > In vivo bioluminescence imaging
text: C57BL/6J mice were administered LNP-Luc mRNA. At T = 4 h post-injection, bioluminescence imaging was carried out as described previously2,11 using an IVIS Spectrum imaging system (Caliper Life Sciences). d-Luciferin sodium salt (Regis Technologies) was administered to mice intraperitoneally at 150 mg/kg. After 5 min, the mice were euthanized; desired tissues were harvested, washed with PBS, and then immediately placed on the imaging platform. With dissections involving BM, femurs were dislodged, cleaned, and lightly crushed with a spatula. Tissue luminescence was measured on the IVIS using an exposure time of 5 s or longer to ensure that the signal obtained was within the operative detection range. Bioluminescence values were also quantified by measuring photon flux (p/s) in the region of interest (ROI) using Living Image software provided by Caliper.

section_path: Materials and methods > Acute systemic inflammatory induction by LPS; IL-6 serum ELISA measurement in C57BL/6J mice
text: C57BL/6J mice were i.v. injected with LPS at 2 mg/kg to reach systemic inflammation as previously reported.67 At T = 4 h post-LPS treatment, mice were i.v. injected with either LNP-mRNA or CD47/LNP-mRNA. At T = 4 h post-injection, peripheral blood was collected in heparin tubes and spun at 1,500 × g for 10 min at 4°C to isolate serum. Concentration of IL-6 in serum was measured by ELISA according to the manufacturer’s protocol (DuoSet ELISA kits, R&D Systems).

section_path: Materials and methods > Determination of in vivo genome editing efficiency of CD47/tLNP-cre mRNA with a Cre/loxP reporter system
text: To assess delivery efficiency to targeted cell populations, mRNA expression upon i.v. administration of LNP-mRNA was traced through single-cell flow cytometry analysis, as reported previously.1,2,3 LNP-Cre was i.v. injected into Ai6 mice, which contain a loxP reporter system to express ZsGreen upon Cre-mediated recombination.

section_path: Materials and methods > Determination of in vivo genome editing efficiency of CD47/tLNP-cre mRNA with a Cre/loxP reporter system
text: To trace mRNA expression in bone marrow (BM), 24 h post-tLNP-Cre treatment, mice were euthanized, femurs were dislodged, and connective tissues were removed with 70% ethanol. Each end of the bone was cut with dissection scissors, and BM was flushed with fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) buffer and passed through a 70-μm filter. Cell pellets underwent 1–2 RBC lysis cycles with ammonium-chloride-potassium (ACK) buffer, followed by ice-cold 2% FACS washes. After centrifugation and removal of supernatant, BM cells were resuspended in FACS buffer and were stained with Live/Dead Aqua cell stain (Thermo Fisher) and anti-mouse antibodies for flow cytometry analysis.

section_path: Materials and methods > Mice treatments for ex vivo GFP+ BMT and LNP-Puma pre-conditioning
text: CD47+aCD117/tLNP or aCD117/tLNP containing Puma mRNA pre-conditioning injections were performed at 1 μg via i.v. administration in C57BL/6 mice. Mice were injected 6.5 days prior to BMT (i.v.) of 10E+06 RBC-depleted GFP+ C57BL/6 CD45.2 BM cells. Mice survival was observed.

section_path: Materials and methods > Preparation of peripheral blood for flow cytometry analysis
text: Peripheral whole blood was collected using heparinized Microhematocrit Capillary Tubes (Fisherbrand) and immediately transferred to blood collection tubes (Becton Dickinson). Flow cytometry was performed on either whole blood or on white blood cells after RBC lysis using ACK buffer at room temperature following the manufacturer’s instructions. Measurement of GFP+ donor cells was performed through flow cytometry analysis.

section_path: Materials and methods > Formation/isolation of LNP-mRNA protein corona
text: Equal volumes of CD47/LNP, scrambled CD47/LNP, or unmodified LNP, in which the LNP was labeled with DiO fluorescent dye, were gently mixed with normal mouse serum (Thermo Fisher) for a total of 0.2 mL volume and incubated for 1 h at 37°C. Protein coronas were purified by size-exclusion Sepharose CL-4B column chromatography (MilliporeSigma). The 0.2-mL fractions positive for LNP as detected through fluorescence intensity (Figure S4) were pooled together, totaling 1.2 mL and frozen on dry ice. Samples were then prepared for LC-MS/MS analysis performed at Bioinformatics Solutions.

section_path: Materials and methods > LC-MS and proteomic analysis of protein corona
text: Protein coronas were reduced with 10 mM DTT (Sigma-Aldrich) alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) chloroform/methanol precipitated and digested with trypsin (Promega). Digested samples were lyophilized. Lyophilized samples were resuspended in 0.2% trifluoroacetic acid and desalted. Samples were injected into the Thermo Orbitrap Exploris 240 (Thermo Fisher) by nanoflow LC using an Ultimate 3000 chromatography system (Thermo Fisher). MS data were acquired on a Thermo Orbitrap Exploris 240. MS RAW files were processed using PEAKS Studio (version 10, Bioinformatics Solutions). The data were searched against the mouse Uniprot-reviewed database. Semi-specific cleavage with trypsin was selected, with a maximum of two missed cleavages. A fixed modification of carbamidomethylation (+57.02 Da) on cysteine residues was specified. Variable modifications of deamidation (+0.98 Da) on asparagine and glutamine and oxidation (15.99 Da) on methionine were specified. The false discovery rate (FDR) threshold was set to 1% for the database search. Absolute abundance in LC-MS is normalized by Z score, and the heatmap was generated by the ComplexHeatmap, with rows clustered by Pearson correlation.

section_path: Materials and methods > RNA-seq analysis of hepatic tissue
text: 10 μg of either unmodified LNP-mRNA, CD47/LNP-mRNA, scrambled peptide/LNP-mRNA or PBS (untreated) was administered i.v. by retro-orbital injection to C57BL/6 mice. Animals were sacrificed at 4 h post-injection, and liver tissue was collected, washed with saline, placed into conical tubes, and immediately frozen on dry ice. The tissue was then processed further for RNA-seq analysis performed by the Gene Expression and Regulation Program Bioinformatics Facility at The Wistar Institute, University of Pennsylvania. RNA-seq data were aligned using the STAR algorithm against mm10 mouse genome version.68 RSEM version t1.2.12 software was used to estimate read counts and reads per kilobase per million mapped reads values using gene information from Ensemble transcriptome version GRCm38.89.69 Raw counts were used to estimate the significance of differential expression differences between two experimental groups using DESeq2.70 Overall gene expression changes were considered significant if they passed the FDR <5% thresholds.
